summary: This paper proposes a hybrid model combining dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) and neural networks (NNs) to forecast and classify the severity progression of COVID-19 patients using vital signs and blood analysis over a 40-hour horizon. The approach forecasts future patient state vectors via DBNs and applies static classifiers to predict critical conditions, outperforming direct classification on initial data.
why_it_matters: Accurately predicting which COVID-19 patients will require intensive care enables better resource allocation and timely medical intervention, improving patient outcomes and healthcare management during pandemics. The hybrid DBN-NN model offers interpretable forecasts and improved classification performance.
method_setup: The model uses a first-order Markovian Gaussian DBN trained on irregularly sampled time series data of vital signs and blood test results from Spanish COVID-19 patients to forecast future states. Subsequently, several static classifiers, including a five-layer dense neural network, classify these forecasted states as critical or non-critical. SMOTE oversampling and g-mean optimization address data imbalance.
key_claims: The hybrid DBN and neural network model achieves better accuracy and g-mean scores than classifiers applied directly to initial patient data.
DBNs effectively forecast future vital signs and blood analysis values in irregularly sampled time series with variable patient stay lengths.
The neural network classifier combined with DBN forecasting improves monotonically over increasing forecast horizons up to 40 hours.
DBNs provide interpretable multivariate probabilistic models revealing relationships among clinical variables influencing forecasts.
The proposed framework is modular and can incorporate different classifier types.
SMOTE oversampling and g-mean metric effectively mitigate class imbalance in critical vs. non-critical patient classification.
limitations: Data is from a specific cohort in Spanish hospitals during the sixth COVID-19 wave, which may limit generalizability.
The dataset has a high proportion of missing data that required substantial preprocessing and variable reduction.
Only patients with multiple time-stamped records were used for DBN training, excluding many cases with single instances.
The forecast horizon is limited to 40 hours due to the chosen sample period and model configuration.
The system's potential response to new viral variants or treatment protocols requires retraining for accuracy.
The dataset and DBN model are complex, possibly limiting real-time deployment in some clinical settings.
